lines: # How to track your spending
> Before you budget or save, find out where your money really goes. Track your spending with a notebook, a spreadsheet or Simple Balance.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/track-your-spending/. Updated 2026-10-25.
Most people have a rough idea of what they spend each month. Tracking your
spending means checking that guess against what really happened. It's the
first step for almost anything else you want to do with your money, from
making a budget to saving for a trip.
## Why it matters
It's hard to change something you can't see. "Spend less" is a wish. "Spend
$150 less on eating out" is a plan, and you can only make it once you know
eating out cost you $450 last month.
Small costs are the easiest to miss. Nobody forgets the rent, but coffee,
delivery fees and the app you tried for free slip by and add up. In a
[2022 survey by C+R Research](https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/),
people first guessed they spent $86 a month on subscriptions. When they were
asked about each kind one at a time, the total came to $219.
Real numbers also make a better budget. Say you set $300 for groceries because
it sounded about right, but you really spend $500. That budget is broken by
the second week, and it's easy to give up on it. A budget built on two months
of real spending starts out believable.
Tracking also tells you whether you're getting ahead. Take what came in,
subtract what went out, and you'll know if your savings grew or shrank. You
need both numbers to know that.
## How to do it
You don't need special software. A notebook or a spreadsheet is fine, and the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has a free
[spending tracker](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_spending_tracker_2018-11_ADA.pdf)
you can print. What matters most is doing the same few steps each time.
### 1. Gather a month or two of statements
Start with your checking account and each credit card. Most banks let you
download statements from their website, often as a spreadsheet file. One full
month is enough to start. Two or three is better, because a single month
usually has something odd in it, like a birthday or a car repair.
### 2. Pick a short list of categories
A category is a label for what the money was for, like groceries or rent.
Start with eight or ten:
- Housing (rent or mortgage)
- Utilities (power, water, phone, internet)
- Groceries
- Eating out
- Transportation (gas, bus fare, car payment)
- Health
- Shopping
- Subscriptions
- Everything else
You can split one up later if it's hiding something. Start with too many and
every receipt turns into a puzzle. [A list of budget categories](https://smpl.money/learn/budget-categories/)
has more ideas.
### 3. Give every purchase a category
Go down each statement and label every purchase. Two kinds of entries are easy
to get wrong, so keep an eye out for them.
The first is money moving between your own accounts. Paying your credit card
from checking doesn't change what you spent, because the spending happened
when you used the card. If you count the card payment as well, you've counted
those groceries twice. Moving money into savings works the same way.

**Diagram: An example: money leaves your accounts once, at the store. Paying the card from checking is a transfer, so the $80 counts once, not twice.** Checking and a credit card sit inside a dashed line marked Your accounts, and a store sits outside it. An arrow marked $80, Spending, goes from the credit card out to the store. An arrow marked $80, Transfer, goes from checking to the credit card and stays inside the line. Counted as spending: $80, not $160.
The second is refunds. If you return $40 of clothes, you spent $40 less on
clothes. That money is coming back, not money you earned, so take it off the
clothes category.
### 4. Add it up
Total each category for the month, then total what came in. Now you can see
where most of your money went, which numbers surprised you, and whether you
spent more than you earned.

**Diagram: An example month: every row gets a category, then each category is added up. The card payment isn’t spending, and the refund comes off Clothes.** Six rows from your statements, each with its category. Grocery store, $80, Groceries. Pizza place, $35, Eating out. Clothing store, $60, Clothes. Card payment, $200, not spending. Grocery store, $45, Groceries. Clothes refund, plus $40, Clothes. Below them, the month’s totals as bars: Groceries $125, made of $80 and $45. Eating out $35. Clothes $60 minus the $40 refund, which is $20. The card payment isn’t in any total.
### 5. Keep it going
Doing this once gives you a snapshot. Doing it every week, for ten or fifteen
minutes, gives you a habit you can use. Weekly is easier than monthly because
you can still remember what most of the charges were.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
Simple Balance is an expense tracker: it keeps your accounts, purchases and
categories in one place and does the adding up for you. It doesn't pull anything from your bank today.
You download the file your bank gives you and bring it in, or type in a
purchase yourself.
### Set up your accounts
Open **Accounts** and press **New account**. Add your checking account and
each credit card, with what each one holds today as the opening balance. For a
credit card, type what you owe as a plain number and leave **Starting balance
type** on **Amount owed**.

![The accounts page: a search box and sort controls, then accounts grouped by type. Under Checking, a euro account at €1,621.10 and Everyday Checking at $7,663.45. Under Savings, Savings at $20,200.00. Under Credit card, a card named Travel Card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/accounts-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Bring in a statement
1. Download your statement from your bank's website as a CSV file, a simple
spreadsheet file that many banks offer.
2. Open **Import CSV**, choose the file, and pick the account it belongs to.
3. Check which column is the date, which is the payee and which is the amount.
Check the date order too. Many US banks put the month first, so 03/04/2026
means March 4.
4. Press **Dry run** to see how each row will be read. Nothing is saved yet.
5. Press **Stage all rows**.

![The import screen before a file is picked: a step headed Choose a CSV file, an empty drop target reading Drop in a file or browse, and a preview panel saying no file has been chosen yet.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/import-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
The rows go to **Staged**, a waiting area where nothing counts toward your
balances yet. If something looks wrong, you can fix it or delete it there, and
no harm is done. [Importing a statement](https://smpl.money/docs/importing-a-statement/) has more
detail.
### Sort the rows as you check them
On **Staged**, click a row's category to set it. If you type a name that
doesn't exist yet, Simple Balance creates it. Rows that look like something
you already have get flagged as possible duplicates, so bringing in the same
statement twice won't double your spending. When everything looks right,
press **Commit selected**.

![Staged transactions, the review queue: four rows that don't count yet, each with a date, payee, account, category, a Ready status and an amount, including a $19.99 refund from Streamly and a $23.50 transit pass on the travel card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/staged-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Card payments and refunds
When you pay your card from checking, record it as a **Transfer**, not a
withdrawal. A transfer moves money between two of your own accounts, so it
never counts as spending. On **Transactions**, a transfer shows both accounts
and no category, like the $600 moved into savings below.
For a refund, choose **Deposit** and give it the same category as the
purchase. That category's spending goes down by the amount of the refund. If
the category is new, the form asks what kind of money it is. Pick **A refund
of money you spent**.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### See where it went
**Overview** shows your spending by category for any dates you choose,
biggest first. Transfers are left out, so a card payment never shows up as
spending.

![The Simple Balance overview for one month: a dollar total with balance, deposits, withdrawals and net cash flow across the top, then a checking account, a savings account and a credit card with their balances, beside spending by category as bars from rent down to subscriptions.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/dashboard-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
**Reports** goes into more detail. The **Categories** report breaks spending
down by category, and **Income and expenses** compares what came in with what
went out. If one big category like rent makes the rest hard to see on the
chart, open its row's menu and choose **Exclude from this view**. That only
changes what you're looking at, not your records.
If you find the same store filed under the wrong category for months, go to
**Transactions**, check those rows, and change their category all at once.
> **Don't forget cash.** Cash never shows up in a bank file, so it's the spending most likely to go
> missing. Save a **template** for cash purchases you make often, like coffee or
> parking, and adding one takes a click.
> [What is envelope budgeting?](https://smpl.money/learn/envelope-budgeting/) shows how to keep
> track of cash as its own account.
Once you have a month or two of real numbers, you're ready to
[make your first budget](https://smpl.money/learn/make-a-budget/).
## Sources
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [Your Money, Your Goals toolkit](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/educator-tool/your-money-your-goals/toolkit/). Updated April 2026.

- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [Spending tracker](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_spending_tracker_2018-11_ADA.pdf), from the Your Money, Your Goals toolkit. 2018.
- C+R Research. [Subscription service statistics and costs](https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/). Survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers, April and May 2022.

lines: # A list of budget categories, with examples
> The categories most households need, what goes in each one, and how many to start with. Then how to set them up in Simple Balance.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/budget-categories/. Updated 2026-10-25.
A budget category is a label for what your money was for, like groceries,
rent or gas. Every purchase gets one. At the end of the month you add up each
label, and you can see where your money went.
The hard part is picking the list. With too few labels, everything ends up in
"Shopping." With too many, you spend more time sorting than you save.
## Why it matters
Your bank statement is a list of store names in the order you visited them,
which doesn't tell you much. Categories turn it into an answer, like "we spent
$640 on food last month, and $260 of it was takeout."
They also let you compare one month with the next. If groceries are always
their own category, you can watch them go up in December and back down in
January. That only works if the names stay the same.
And categories are what a budget is built on. You can't set a limit for
eating out until eating out has a category of its own.
## Where most people's money goes
A few categories take up most of the money. In 2024 the average U.S. household
spent $78,535, according to the
[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cesan.nr0.htm).
A third of that went to housing, about 17% to getting around, and about 13% to
food. More of the food money went to groceries than to eating out. Together,
those three made up more than 60% of all spending. Your own numbers will be
different, but those are the categories to set up first.

**Diagram: Where the average U.S. household’s money went in 2024, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Housing, getting around and food took more than 60% of it.** Bars showing how the average U.S. household’s $78,535 of spending in 2024 was shared out, largest first: housing 33.4%, getting around (transportation) 17.0%, food 12.9% (7.9% on groceries and 5.0% on eating out), Social Security and retirement, mostly taken out of pay (the survey calls it personal insurance and pensions), 12.5%, healthcare 7.9%, entertainment 4.6%, everything else, such as personal care, 4.2%, gifts and donations (the survey calls them cash contributions) 2.9%, clothes and shoes 2.5%, and education 2.0%. The first three are boxed together and marked as more than 60% of all spending. Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditures, 2024.
## A starter list
Most people need something close to this list. It's a lot like the one on the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's
[budget worksheet](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_well-being_monthly-budget.pdf).
You don't need every line, and you can rename anything.
**Home**
- Rent or mortgage
- Utilities: power, gas, water, trash
- Phone and internet
- Renters or homeowners insurance
- Repairs and supplies
**Food**
- Groceries
- Eating out, including takeout and coffee
**Getting around**
- Car payment
- Gas and charging
- Car insurance
- Car repairs and registration
- Bus, train and rideshare
**Health**
- Health insurance you pay for yourself
- Doctor, dentist and eye care
- Prescriptions
**Family and pets**
- Childcare
- Kids' activities and school costs
- Pet food and vet bills
**Personal**
- Clothes and shoes
- Haircuts and personal care
- Gifts and donations
**Fun**
- Streaming and other subscriptions
- Hobbies and going out
- Travel
**Everything else**
- Bank fees and interest
- Other
Keep the list for money coming in short: your paycheck, any side work, and
interest. A refund doesn't need an income category. It goes back into the
category you spent it from, as
[how to track your spending](https://smpl.money/learn/track-your-spending/) explains.
## How to pick your categories
### 1. Start from your own statements
Look at a month or two of real spending before you choose. A list copied from
somewhere else will have categories you never use and miss some you need.
### 2. Start with about ten
You can always add more later. Ten labels are easy to keep up with. Thirty
make every receipt a decision.
### 3. Split a category when it's hiding something
"Food" works fine until you want to know how much of it is takeout. That's when
to split it into Groceries and Eating out. If you never wonder, you don't need
the split.

**Diagram: As one Food category, all you can see is that you spent $640. Split it in two, and you can see that $260 of it was eating out.** Two bars of the same length. The first is one category, Food, at $640. The second is the same money split into two categories: Groceries at $380 and Eating out at $260. A dashed line marks where the split falls, and below it, $380 plus $260 equals $640.
### 4. Decide the tricky ones once
One trip to a big store might be food, cleaning supplies and a shirt. A phone
bill might be personal or for work. Choose a rule the first time and stick to
it, so the same thing lands in the same place every month.
### 5. Leave transfers out
Paying your credit card or moving money into savings isn't spending. If you
give it a spending category, you'll count the same money twice.
### 6. Keep an eye on "Other"
A little in Other is fine. If it becomes one of your biggest categories,
something in there deserves its own name.
### 7. Group them for the big picture
Ten categories are easier to read as three or four groups, like Home, Food and
Fun. You can then budget a whole group at once, or each category in it.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
You don't have to set up categories first. Type a new name in the category box
when you add a transaction, and Simple Balance creates it. Bring in a bank file
that has a category column, and those names come in too.
When you type a new category name on a deposit, the form asks what kind of
money it is. Choose **Money you earned** for pay. Choose **A refund of money
you spent** for a refund, so it lowers your spending instead of counting as
income.
### Set them up ahead of time
Open [**Categories**](https://smpl.money/docs/categories-and-payees/). In the form for a new
category, type a **Category name** and choose what it **Applies to**:
**Expense**, **Income**, or **Income or expense**. Then press **Add category**.

![The categories page: a form for a new category with its name, what it applies to and its group, a panel for making groups with no groups yet, and the list of categories below, each with its type, how many transactions use it and a group picker, starting with Dining out, Freelance and Groceries.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/categories-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Make groups
On the same page, type a **Group name** and press **Add group**. You'll also
choose how the group is budgeted. **Has a budget of its own** means one number
for the whole group. **Adds up its categories' budgets** means you budget each
category inside it, and the group shows the total.
Then use the group picker on each category's row to put it in a group. Moving
a category changes the group's totals for past months too, so you can
rearrange your groups whenever you like.
### Clean up
If you end up with two categories for the same thing, like Dining and Eating
out, check the box next to each on **Categories**. Choose the one to keep and
press **Merge**. Every transaction moves to the one you kept.
To change the category on lots of purchases at once, go to
[**Transactions**](https://smpl.money/docs/transactions/), check the rows, and change them
together. When one receipt covers two categories, press **Split across
categories** in the transaction form and give each part its own amount.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
A category you've stopped using can be archived from its row. It leaves the
list, but its history stays. Turn on **Show archived** to see it again.
### See where the money went
[**Overview**](https://smpl.money/docs/the-overview/) shows spending by category for any dates you
pick. The **Categories** report under [**Reports**](https://smpl.money/docs/reports/) goes into
more detail. Transfers between your own accounts don't show up in either,
because they don't have a category.

![The Simple Balance overview for one month: a dollar total with balance, deposits, withdrawals and net cash flow across the top, then a checking account, a savings account and a credit card with their balances, beside spending by category as bars from rent down to subscriptions.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/dashboard-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
Once your categories feel right, [make a budget](https://smpl.money/learn/make-a-budget/) from
them.
## Sources
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. [Consumer Expenditures, 2024](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cesan.nr0.htm). News release, December 19, 2025.
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [Monthly budget worksheet](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_well-being_monthly-budget.pdf).

lines: # How to make a budget
> A budget is a plan for your money, made before the month starts. Make your first one from real numbers, and keep it going after the first month.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/make-a-budget/. Updated 2026-10-25.
A budget is a plan for what your money will do this month, made before the
month starts. You write down a few numbers, check them against what really
happens, and fix the ones that turn out wrong. It doesn't have to be strict,
and you don't fill it in once and forget it.
## Why it matters
With a budget, you decide once instead of at every checkout. Without one,
each purchase is a new choice made on the spot, often when you're tired or
hungry. A budget lets you make those choices ahead of time, when you're calm.
It also shows you the trade-offs. Money spent on one thing can't be spent on
something else. If you want $100 more for eating out, it has to come from
somewhere, and a budget lets you pick where.
You catch problems early, too. If you notice in the second week that groceries
are running high, you still have time to adjust. If you only find out when the
card bill comes, the month is already over.
And saving stops being whatever's left over. When saving is a line in your
budget, it happens. When it's whatever remains at the end of the month, there's
often nothing left.
## How to do it
These steps cover the same ground as the Consumer Financial Protection
Bureau's
[guide to making a budget](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/budgeting-how-to-create-a-budget-and-stick-with-it/):
what comes in, what goes out, and when your bills are due. Its
[budget worksheet](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_well-being_monthly-budget.pdf)
is a handy place to write it all down.
### 1. Start from what you take home
Use the amount that lands in your account after taxes and anything else your
employer takes out, not your salary. If your pay changes from month to month,
plan around a low month instead of an average one.
[How to budget with irregular income](https://smpl.money/learn/budget-with-irregular-income/)
covers that in more detail.
### 2. Write down the fixed bills
These are the bills that stay about the same every month: rent or mortgage,
utilities, insurance, your phone, the minimum payment on any debt, and the
subscriptions you're keeping.
### 3. Look at what everything else really costs
Groceries, eating out, gas, shopping and fun change from month to month. Don't
guess at them. Use the last two or three months of statements, which is what
[tracking your spending](https://smpl.money/learn/track-your-spending/) gives you. A budget
built on guesses tends to fall apart in the first week.
### 4. Set a number for each category
Start each one at about what you spend now. Then change a few on purpose: the
ones you want to bring down, and any goals you want to save for. It's easier
to stick with two or three changes than with fifteen.
### 5. Plan for the months that aren't typical
Car insurance twice a year, holidays, birthdays, new tires. These are easy to
leave out because they don't happen every month, and then they show up all at
once. [Utah State University Extension](https://extension.usu.edu/finance/faq/budget-for-non-monthly-expenses)
suggests adding up a year of these bills, dividing by 12, and setting that
much aside each month. That's what [sinking funds](https://smpl.money/learn/sinking-funds/) are
for.
### 6. Check in every week
Ten minutes a week is enough. Compare what you've spent so far with each
number. When a category runs over, take the difference from another category,
or accept it and move on. Change the numbers when you need to, but keep the
spending you record honest. A budget only works if it's checked against what
you really spent.

**Diagram: An example check-in. Eating out ran $30 over, so $30 of the fun budget moves to cover it. The two budgets still add up to $180.** Two budgets, before and after a weekly check-in, each drawn as a bar with a line where its budget ends. Green is what was spent within the budget, and red is what was spent over it. Before: eating out has a $100 budget and $130 spent, so it’s $30 over. Fun has an $80 budget and $20 spent, so it has $60 left, and $30 of what’s left is outlined. An arrow moves that $30 of the fun budget to eating out. After: eating out has a $130 budget and $130 spent, with $0 left, and its whole bar is green. Fun has a $50 budget and $20 spent, with $30 left. Together the two budgets are still $180.
### 7. Expect the first few months to be off
Your first budget is still partly a guess. By the third month, real spending
has corrected most of the numbers, and the budget starts to feel like it fits.
> **Pick a method later, if at all.** There are named ways to budget, such as
> [zero-based budgeting](https://smpl.money/learn/zero-based-budgeting/) and
> [envelopes](https://smpl.money/learn/envelope-budgeting/). Each one is a different answer to how
> strict to be. You don't need one to start. A number for each category is
> already a budget.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
In Simple Balance, a budget compares what you planned to spend in a category
with what you actually spent. A budget never changes your balances, so
deleting one changes nothing else.
### Start with real spending
Bring in a month or two of statements first, or type them in, so your budget
starts from real numbers. [How to track your spending](https://smpl.money/learn/track-your-spending/)
shows how. Then **Overview** shows your spending by category, so you can see
what each one really costs.

![The Simple Balance overview for one month: a dollar total with balance, deposits, withdrawals and net cash flow across the top, then a checking account, a savings account and a credit card with their balances, beside spending by category as bars from rent down to subscriptions.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/dashboard-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Set a budget
Open **Budgets**. Under **Set a budget**, choose a category, type the monthly
amount, pick the date it starts, and press **Set budget**. That one budget
covers every month from then on until you end it, so there's nothing to set up
again next month.

![The budgets screen: a form for setting one, with fields for the category, the amount and how it's decided, the currency, a start date and an optional end date, an optional savings goal and which budget gets funded first, and a checkbox for carrying what's left into next month. Below it, the list of standing budgets begins with $200 a month for dining out.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/budgets-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Read your budget
Each budget gets a row. **Budget** is your limit, **Spent** is what you've
spent, and **Remaining** is the difference. A refund lowers **Spent**, since
it gives back money you'd spent. A month that isn't over yet is marked **So
far**, because being under budget halfway through the month doesn't mean
you'll finish under.

**Diagram: An example month that isn’t over yet. Groceries is under its budget so far. Eating out has already gone $30 over, so its bar is full and red.** Two budget rows for October, halfway through the month, so the month is marked so far. Each row has a badge, then a bar that ends at a line for the budget. The whole bar is the budget, the filled part is what’s been spent, and the empty part is what remains. Groceries: a budget of $400, $260 spent, $140 remaining, marked So far, with its bar about two-thirds full and green. Eating out: a budget of $100, $130 spent, so remaining is minus $30, marked Over, and its bar is full and red.
Spending in categories you haven't budgeted shows up too, so you can see where
the rest of your money went. A category you budgeted but didn't spend anything
in still shows, at zero.
### Let one month be different
December's grocery bill isn't the same as November's. Press the calendar
button at the end of a budget's row to set an amount for just that month.
Clear it later to go back to the usual amount.
### A simple first month
Set budgets on your five biggest spending categories at about what they cost
now. On the two you most want to control, check **Carry what is left over into
the next month**, so money you don't spend stays put for later. For the next
big bill you know is coming, set a budget and fill in **Saving up for** and
**Needed by**. Then
come back once a week. The [Budgets](https://smpl.money/docs/budgets/) page in the
documentation has more detail.
## Sources

- Courtney-Rose Dantus, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [Budgeting: How to create a budget and stick with it](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/budgeting-how-to-create-a-budget-and-stick-with-it/). June 5, 2019.

articles.description: Zero-based budgeting means deciding what every dollar you have is for, until no money is left without a plan. Your bank balance doesn't go to zero.

lines: # What is zero-based budgeting?
> Zero-based budgeting means deciding what every dollar you have is for, until no money is left without a plan. Your bank balance doesn't go to zero.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/zero-based-budgeting/. Updated 2026-10-25.
In a zero-based budget, you decide what every dollar you have is for: rent,
groceries, the emergency fund, next summer's trip. You keep going until there's
no money left without a plan.
## What it is
The idea started in business. Peter Pyhrr wrote about it in a 1970
[_Harvard Business Review_ article](https://www.econbiz.de/Record/zero-base-budgeting-pyhrr-peter/10002660711)
called "Zero-Base Budgeting." Instead of starting from last year's budget,
every cost starts at zero and has to earn its place.
At home it's simpler. Suzanne Holloway, an extension agent at the University of
Florida, [describes it](https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/leonco/2025/09/12/budgeting-basics/) as a budget that "assigns every dollar earned a
purpose." You can think of each purpose as a job for that money. In numbers,
it looks like this:
**Money coming in, minus every dollar you've assigned, equals zero.**
The zero is the money without a plan. Your bank balance doesn't go to zero.
Say you have $3,000 in checking. You might assign $1,400 to rent, $500 to
groceries, $300 to the car, $200 to fun and $600 to savings. Nothing is left
unassigned, but the money is all still there. It's just spoken for.

**Diagram: Every dollar of the $3,000 gets a job, so nothing is left to assign. The money is still in checking. It’s just spoken for.** A bar for the $3,000 in checking, filled from end to end by five jobs: rent $1,400, groceries $500, car $300, fun $200 and savings $600. Below it, the sum: in checking $3,000, minus $3,000 given a job, leaves $0 to assign. The checking balance is still $3,000.
## Why it matters
Money without a job tends to get spent on whatever comes up. Giving it a job
before the month starts keeps that from happening.
Savings gets a job like everything else. In a zero-based budget, the
[emergency fund](https://smpl.money/learn/emergency-fund/) isn't whatever's left over at the end.
It's a line you put money into, just like rent.
When you overspend, the money has to come from somewhere. If groceries run $60
over, you take $60 from another job. That makes it a choice you make on
purpose, not a surprise at the end of the month.

**Diagram: When groceries run $60 over, the $60 comes from another job, here fun. The money only moved between jobs, so left to assign stays at $0.** Two columns, groceries and fun. Groceries ran $60 over its $500. An arrow carries a $60 piece from the top of fun’s column, where a dashed outline marks the gap it left, to the top of groceries’ column. Groceries becomes $500 plus $60, which is $560. Fun becomes $200 minus $60, which is $140. Left to assign stays at $0.
It also works when your pay changes. You only assign money you already have,
so a small month just means fewer jobs get money.
## How to do it
### 1. Start with the money you have
Use what's in your accounts now, or this month's pay once it arrives. Only
budget money you already have, not money you're expecting.
### 2. List the jobs
Put the fixed bills first, then everyday needs like groceries and gas, then
savings goals and extra debt payments, then the fun stuff. Bills that don't
come every month, like insurance or holiday gifts, get a little money each
month too.
### 3. Assign money until nothing is left
Go down the list and give each job an amount. If you run out of money before
you reach the end, the last items wait until next time. If money is left
after the last item, give it a job too, like extra savings or paying down a
debt.
### 4. Move money when plans change
When a category runs over, take the difference from another one and write
down that you did. Most of zero-based budgeting is this one habit.
### 5. Give new money a job right away
A refund, a gift or money from a side job gets a job the day it arrives.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
To use Simple Balance as a zero-based budgeting app, two features work
together. One is budgets that
carry over from month to month. The other is a number called **left to
assign**.
### Turn on carrying
On **Budgets**, when you set or edit a budget, check **Carry what is left over
into the next month**. That turns the budget into an envelope. Whatever you
don't spend this month is added to next month, and anything you overspend is
taken off next month.

![The budgets screen: a form for setting one, with fields for the category, the amount and how it's decided, the currency, a start date and an optional end date, an optional savings goal and which budget gets funded first, and a checkbox for carrying what's left into next month. Below it, the list of standing budgets begins with $200 a month for dining out.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/budgets-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Watch what's left to assign
Once any budget carries over, the **Budgets** page shows how much is **left to
assign**. That's the money in the accounts your budget covers, minus what your
envelopes already hold. Your goal is to bring it to zero by giving the rest a
job.
### Choose which accounts count
Each account's form has a box called **The budget is about the money in this
account**. Leave it on for checking, savings you spend from, and credit cards.
Card spending empties an envelope right away, even though the cash leaves
later when you pay the bill. Turn the box off for money that isn't part of
your plan, like a retirement account.
Your accounts are on the **Accounts** page, grouped by type. The box is in each
account's form.

![The accounts page: a search box and sort controls, then accounts grouped by type. Under Checking, a euro account at €1,621.10 and Everyday Checking at $7,663.45. Under Savings, Savings at $20,200.00. Under Credit card, a card named Travel Card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/accounts-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Move money between jobs
When one category runs over and you want to cover it from another, change both
amounts for this month only. Press the calendar button at the end of each
budget's row and type the new amount. Next month, both go back to normal.
### Set a limit on an envelope
**Most to carry** stops an envelope from growing forever. It works both ways.
It caps money that piles up in a fund you never use, and it caps overspending
that never gets paid back.
[What is envelope budgeting?](https://smpl.money/learn/envelope-budgeting/) looks at the same
idea from another angle. The [Budgets](https://smpl.money/docs/budgets/) page in the
documentation explains exactly how left to assign is worked out.
## Sources

- Peter A. Pyhrr. "Zero-Base Budgeting." _Harvard Business Review_ 48, no. 6 (November and December 1970): 111 to 121. [Library record](https://www.econbiz.de/Record/zero-base-budgeting-pyhrr-peter/10002660711).
- Suzanne Holloway, UF/IFAS Extension Leon County. [The Basics to Budgeting](https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/leonco/2025/09/12/budgeting-basics/). September 12, 2025.

articles.title: What is envelope budgeting?
articles.description: Cash in labeled envelopes, and when one is empty you stop. How the envelope method works, how to do it without cash, and how to keep track of cash you do spend.
steps: Put a limit on an envelope
See what's left to put in envelopes
lines: # What is envelope budgeting?
> Cash in labeled envelopes, and when one is empty you stop. How the envelope method works, how to do it without cash, and how to keep track of cash you do spend.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/envelope-budgeting/. Updated 2026-10-25.
The classic version of envelope budgeting uses real envelopes. On payday you
take out cash and split it into envelopes labeled Groceries, Gas and Fun. You
spend from each one until it's empty, and then you stop. You may also hear it
called "cash stuffing."
## What it is
Suzanne Holloway, an extension agent at the University of Florida,
[describes the method](https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/leonco/2025/09/12/budgeting-basics/)
as using "physical or digital envelopes for each spending category." Once an
envelope is empty, you stop spending in that category "until the next budget
period." In practice, that comes down to two rules:
1. **Each envelope holds the money for one kind of spending.** Grocery money
comes from the grocery envelope and nowhere else.
2. **What's left at the end of the month stays in the envelope.** With cash,
it's still sitting there, so it doesn't go back into one big pile. If you
spent $340 from a $400 grocery envelope, next month starts with $60 already
in it.

**Diagram: What you don’t spend stays in the envelope. Next month starts with that $60, so if you put in $400 again, you have $460 for groceries.** Two bars for a grocery envelope. This month, $400 went in: $340 was spent and $60 is left. An arrow carries the $60 down to next month, which starts with that $60 and gets $400 more on payday, $460 in all.
The second rule is what sets envelopes apart from a budget that starts over
every month.
## Why it matters
The limit feels real. A number on a spreadsheet is easy to ignore, but an
empty envelope is hard to argue with. Even if you never touch cash, sticking
to "empty means stop" is what gives the budget teeth.
Spending less one month pays off the next. Because leftovers stay put, spending
less on gas in March gives you more for gas in April. In a budget that resets
every month, that saving just disappears.
You can see what overspending costs you. If you borrow from the Fun envelope
to cover groceries, you know exactly how much less fun you're having.
It also helps with costs that don't come every month. An envelope for car
repairs that gets $50 a month and sits untouched for a year has $600 in it
when the brakes go.

**Diagram: An envelope can save up for a cost that doesn’t come every month. Put in $50 a month and leave it alone, and after a year it holds $600.** Twelve bars, one for each month, each taller than the one before. A car repair envelope gets $50 a month and nothing is taken out, so it holds $50 after the first month and $600 after the twelfth, when the brakes go.
## How to do it
### 1. Choose which spending gets an envelope
Envelopes work best for spending that changes from month to month and that you
control, like groceries, eating out, gas, household supplies and personal
spending. Bills paid automatically, like rent or insurance, can stay in your
checking account.
### 2. Decide how much goes in each
Use what you've actually spent over the last few months.
[How to track your spending](https://smpl.money/learn/track-your-spending/) shows you how to
find that out.
### 3. Fill the envelopes on payday
With cash, that means a trip to the bank. A Utah State University Extension
guide, [Dam that Cash Flow!](https://extension.usu.edu/archive/dam-that-cash-flow),
puts it simply: cash the check and put the money for each expense in its own
marked envelope. Without cash, you write down how much of your checking
balance belongs to each envelope.
### 4. Spend only from the right envelope
When one runs out, stop. If you really need more, move money from another
envelope on purpose and write down that you did.
### 5. Keep the leftovers
Don't sweep what's left back into one pile. Leave it in its envelope, or move
it to an envelope for something you're saving toward.
> **Cash has costs too.** Cash can be lost or stolen, and it earns nothing sitting in an envelope.
> Paying bills online with it is awkward, too. You can keep cash envelopes for a
> few everyday categories and use your bank account for the rest. Or skip the
> cash and keep the envelopes as numbers.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
To use Simple Balance as an envelope budgeting app, make each envelope a
budget that carries over.
### Make a budget carry over
On [**Budgets**](https://smpl.money/docs/budgets/), set a budget on a category and check **Carry
what is left over into the next month**. If you don't spend $50 of your grocery
budget in March, you have $50 more for groceries in April. Overspending carries
over too. It comes off next month's amount instead of being forgotten when the
month ends.

![The budgets screen: a form for setting one, with fields for the category, the amount and how it's decided, the currency, a start date and an optional end date, an optional savings goal and which budget gets funded first, and a checkbox for carrying what's left into next month. Below it, the list of standing budgets begins with $200 a month for dining out.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/budgets-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Put a limit on an envelope
**Most to carry** limits how much an envelope can hold, in both directions. An
envelope you never touch can't grow forever, and one you keep overspending
can't sink forever.
### See what's left to put in envelopes
Once a budget carries over, the **Budgets** page shows what's **left to
assign**. That's the money in the accounts your budget covers, minus what your
envelopes already hold. It's like the cash you haven't put into an envelope
yet. Bringing it to zero is [zero-based budgeting](https://smpl.money/learn/zero-based-budgeting/).
### Keep track of real cash
If you do use cash, add an account of type **Cash** for your wallet or your
envelopes. Taking money out at an ATM is a **Transfer** from checking to Cash,
since it's still your money. Spending it is a **Withdrawal** from Cash with a
category, and that's what counts against the envelope. In the list below, the
$600 moved from checking to savings is a transfer: it shows both accounts and
no category.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Make cash quick to record
Cash never shows up in a bank file, so it's the spending most likely to go
missing. Save a [**template**](https://smpl.money/docs/templates/) for cash purchases you make
often. Open the menu on any transaction and choose **Save as template**. Next
time, pick the template in the transaction form and it fills itself in. If you
leave the amount blank, it asks you for one each time.

![The templates page before any are saved: a New template button, and a note that you can also choose Save as template from any transaction's menu.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/templates-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
## Sources
- Suzanne Holloway, UF/IFAS Extension Leon County. [The Basics to Budgeting](https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/leonco/2025/09/12/budgeting-basics/). September 12, 2025.
- Adrie Roberts, Utah State University Extension. [Dam that Cash Flow!](https://extension.usu.edu/archive/dam-that-cash-flow). 2004.

articles.description: A sinking fund is money you set aside a little each month for a bill you know is coming, like car insurance in June or gifts in December.

lines: # What are sinking funds?
> A sinking fund is money you set aside a little each month for a bill you know is coming, like car insurance in June or gifts in December.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/sinking-funds/. Updated 2026-10-25.
A sinking fund is money you set aside each month for a bill you know is coming
but don't pay every month. Instead of finding $600 for car insurance in June,
you put away $100 a month starting in January.
## What it is
The name comes from business. When a company borrows money by selling bonds, a
sinking fund is how it pays them back a little at a time instead of all at
once. [FINRA explains bonds](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/bonds)
if you're curious. In a household budget, a sinking fund is the same idea:
**a known amount, needed by a known date, saved in equal pieces**.

**Diagram: Put away $100 a month from January, and the fund reaches $600 in June, the month the bill is due. Then the fund pays the bill.** A bar for each month from January to June, each one a stack of $100 pieces: $100 in January, $200 in February, $300 in March, $400 in April, $500 in May and $600 in June. A dashed line marks the $600 car insurance bill, and the June bar reaches it exactly. An arrow from the June bar pays the bill, drawn as a $600 bar of its own.
It's different from an [emergency fund](https://smpl.money/learn/emergency-fund/). An emergency
fund covers things you can't predict, like losing a job or getting in a car
accident. A sinking fund covers things you can. The holidays come every
December.
Common sinking funds include:
- Car insurance, registration and upkeep
- Holiday and birthday gifts
- A vacation
- Yearly subscriptions and memberships
- Back-to-school costs
- Medical bills up to your insurance deductible
- A new phone or laptop
- Vet bills
## Why it matters
Bills that don't come every month are easy to forget. A monthly budget can look
fine for eleven months, and then the car insurance bill shows up. Without a
sinking fund, that bill often goes on a credit card, and you start the next
month behind.
Small amounts are easier to handle than big ones. Setting aside $75 a month is
one more line in your budget. Finding $900 in December is a scramble.
And when the bill comes, you're ready. Paying it from money you saved for it
means your plan worked.
## How to do it
### 1. List the bills for the next twelve months
Look through last year's statements for anything you paid once or twice:
insurance, renewals, gifts, trips. The list may be longer than you expect.
### 2. Work out the monthly amount
Divide each bill by the number of months until it's due. For bills that come
once a year, [Utah State University Extension](https://extension.usu.edu/finance/faq/budget-for-non-monthly-expenses)
and Oregon's
[Division of Financial Regulation](https://dfr.oregon.gov/financial/manage/pages/budget.aspx)
suggest the same thing: divide by 12 and set that much aside every month.
| Bill          | Amount | Due in    | Each month |
| Car insurance | $600   | 6 months  | $100       |
| Holidays      | $900   | 10 months | $90        |
| Vet checkup   | $240   | 12 months | $20        |

**Diagram: Each bill is cut into one equal piece for every month until it’s due. The holidays cost the most, but with 10 months to save, each piece is smaller than car insurance’s.** Three bars on the same scale, each cut into equal monthly pieces. Car insurance, $600 due in 6 months: 6 pieces of $100. Holidays, $900 due in 10 months: 10 pieces of $90. Vet checkup, $240 due in 12 months: 12 pieces of $20.
The later you start a fund, the more you have to save each month. That's a
good reason to start all of them now.
### 3. Set the money aside
You can move it into a separate savings account. Or you can leave it in
checking and keep a list of how much belongs to each fund. Either way works,
as long as you don't count that money as free to spend.
### 4. Pay the bill from the fund
When the bill comes, the money is waiting. Pay it, then start saving again for
next time.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
A budget in Simple Balance can save toward a date on its own.
### Set the goal
On [**Budgets**](https://smpl.money/docs/budgets/), under **Set a budget**, choose the category
you'll pay the bill from, like Car insurance. Type the bill's amount in **Saving
up for**. A **Needed by** box then appears: type the due date there, not in
**Ends after**.

![The budgets screen: a form for setting one, with fields for the category, the amount and how it's decided, the currency, a start date and an optional end date, an optional savings goal and which budget gets funded first, and a checkbox for carrying what's left into next month. Below it, the list of standing budgets begins with $200 a month for dining out.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/budgets-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Let it work out the amount
You don't type a monthly amount. Each month, the budget figures out what's still
needed and divides it by the months left before the due date. The amount changes
as the fund fills up, and it stops asking once the fund is full. **Carry what is
left over into the next month** is turned on for you, since a fund has to keep
what it saves.
[Saving goals, automatic amounts and the forecast](https://smpl.money/docs/planning-ahead/#how-much-each-month-asks-for)
in the docs shows exactly how each month's amount is worked out.
### Pay the bill from the same category
When the insurance bill comes, record it in the Car insurance category. The
money the budget set aside covers it.
### Know where the money is
A fund is money in your accounts that's set aside for one job. The **Budgets**
page shows what's **left to assign** after every fund and envelope has taken
its share, which tells you how much is really free to spend. If you keep the
fund in a separate savings account, leave **The budget is about the money in
this account** turned on for that account, so its money still counts.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### One fund for each bill
Each fund belongs to the category it's saving for. Holiday gifts, insurance and
a vacation each get their own budget, and each works out its own monthly
amount.
## Sources
- FINRA. [Bonds](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/bonds).
- Melanie Dabb, Utah State University Extension. [How do I budget for non-monthly expenses?](https://extension.usu.edu/finance/faq/budget-for-non-monthly-expenses). October 13, 2020.
- Oregon Division of Financial Regulation. [Creating a personal budget](https://dfr.oregon.gov/financial/manage/pages/budget.aspx).

Let a budget follow your history
lines: # How to budget with irregular income
> When your pay changes from month to month, from freelance work, tips or commission, plan around your lowest month and the money you already have.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/budget-with-irregular-income/. Updated 2026-10-25.
A lot of budgeting advice assumes the same paycheck lands on the same day every
month. If you freelance, work for tips or commission, run a small business, or
get paid every other week, your pay doesn't work that way. You can still
budget. You just plan up from your worst month instead of down from your
average one.
## Why it matters
Budgeting from your average month leaves you short in the slow months. Say you
earned $3,000 one month and $5,000 the next. Planning to spend $4,000 works in
the good month and falls short in the bad one. The bad month is the one where
spending ends up on a credit card.

**Diagram: Budget from your average and the slow month comes up $1,000 short. Budget from your floor, your lowest month, and both months are covered, and the good month’s extra $2,000 can go to your cushion.** Two charts of the same two months: a slow month that brings in $3,000 and a good month that brings in $5,000. A dashed line in each shows the plan. In the first, the plan is the average, $4,000 a month, and the slow month’s bar stops below it, $1,000 short. In the second, the plan is the floor, $3,000 a month. The slow month’s bar reaches it exactly, with a check mark, and the good month’s bar rises $2,000 past it, marked as going to the cushion.
Good months can disappear, too. Without a plan, a big month feels like a raise
and gets spent like one. Then a slow month comes and there's nothing set
aside.
Taxes can be a surprise. If nobody takes tax out of what you're paid, as with
most freelance work, part of every payment isn't yours to spend.
## How to do it
### 1. Find your floor
Look at the last six months and find the month you earned the least. That's
your floor, the amount you can count on.
[Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/budgeting-with-irregular-income)
suggests using exactly that number as your expected income.
### 2. Make a bare-bones budget that fits under it
List rent, utilities, groceries, transportation, insurance and minimum debt
payments. These essentials should fit inside your lowest month. If they don't,
work on that first, because no budgeting method can fix it.
### 3. Rank everything else
Write down what gets money next, in order. For example: a cushion of savings,
then extra debt payments, then the fun stuff. In a good month you get further
down the list. In a slow month you stop sooner, and you already know where.
### 4. Set aside money for taxes first
If you work for yourself, there's no employer
[taking tax out for you](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/self-employed-individuals-tax-center).
If you expect to owe $1,000 or more when you file, the IRS generally wants you
to pay [estimated tax](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/estimated-taxes)
during the year, in four payments. Put part of every payment into a separate
account before you budget the rest. How much depends on where you live and how
much you earn, so it's worth asking a tax preparer once.
### 5. Build a cushion, then budget from last month
[Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/budgeting-with-irregular-income)
suggests an [emergency fund](https://smpl.money/learn/emergency-fund/) of at least one to three
months of your average income. It also suggests keeping the extra from bigger
paychecks as a cushion for the smaller ones. Once your cushion covers a month of
spending, you can budget each month from what you earned the month before. You
always know the amount before the month starts, because the money is already in
the bank. Getting there usually takes a few months of saving extra from the good
ones.
### 6. If you're paid every two weeks
Every two weeks works out to 26 paychecks a year. So in most years,
[two months have three paydays](https://financeadmin.lehigh.edu/content/semi-monthly-bi-weekly-faq)
instead of two. Budget each month on two paychecks, and treat the third as
extra. Put it toward savings, a debt, or your cushion.

**Diagram: One example year, paid every other Friday. Budget each month on two paychecks. Two months get a third one, and that one is extra.** A strip of the twelve months, January to December, with a block for each payday. Every month has two blocks, 24 in all, and a dashed line across the top of the second marks what to budget on. January and July each have a third block above the line, labeled extra, which makes 26 paychecks in the year.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
### Record income as it comes in
Each payment is a **Deposit** with an income category, like Freelance or Tips.
If you're paid on a schedule, set it up once on
[**Recurring**](https://smpl.money/docs/recurring-transactions/). It can repeat every two weeks as
well as every month. If the amount changes, leave it blank. On each payday, a
row shows up in [**Staged**](https://smpl.money/docs/staged-transactions/) for you to fill in with
the real amount.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Budget from last month's income
On [**Budgets**](https://smpl.money/docs/budgets/), under **Amount decided by**, choose **A share
of the income before it**. Then a rule like "groceries get 15% of what came in
last month" sets the budget for you each month. It uses last month because a
share of a month that's still going would keep changing.
### Decide what gets paid first
Give your most important budgets a **Funded first** number. Lower numbers go
first. The **Budgets** page then shows how much of each budget the month's
income covers, filling them in your order until the money runs out. Put rent
and groceries first, and in a slow month you'll see exactly which budgets
didn't get covered.

![The budgets screen: a form for setting one, with fields for the category, the amount and how it's decided, the currency, a start date and an optional end date, an optional savings goal and which budget gets funded first, and a checkbox for carrying what's left into next month. Below it, the list of standing budgets begins with $200 a month for dining out.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/budgets-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Let a budget follow your history
Choose **What the last few periods spent** under **Amount decided by**, and
the budget becomes the average of your last few months. That suits spending
that rises and falls with your income.
### Look ahead
The **What happens next** panel on **Budgets** projects your balances month by
month. It starts from what your accounts hold today and adds your recurring
transactions and what you usually earn and spend. None of it has happened yet.
It's a picture of where things are headed if nothing changes.
[Saving goals, automatic amounts and the forecast](https://smpl.money/docs/planning-ahead/) in the
docs explains each of these in more detail.
## Sources
- Christina Pulman and Denise Continenza, Penn State Extension. [Budgeting with Irregular Income](https://extension.psu.edu/budgeting-with-irregular-income). Updated April 22, 2025.
- Internal Revenue Service. [Self-employed individuals tax center](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/self-employed-individuals-tax-center).
- Internal Revenue Service. [Estimated taxes](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/estimated-taxes).
- Lehigh University Finance and Administration. [Semi-monthly to Bi-weekly FAQ](https://financeadmin.lehigh.edu/content/semi-monthly-bi-weekly-faq).

articles.description: Why your own number and your bank's don't always agree, how to find the difference line by line, and why it's worth ten minutes a month.
steps: Fix it and keep the history
lines: # How to balance your checking account
> Why your own number and your bank's don't always agree, how to find the difference line by line, and why it's worth ten minutes a month.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/balance-your-checking-account/. Updated 2026-10-25.
Balancing your checking account means comparing your own record with your
bank's statement, line by line, until the two agree. Accountants call it
reconciling. People used to do it with a checkbook and a pencil. You may not
write checks anymore, but the reasons to do it haven't gone away.
## Why it matters
You catch charges you didn't make. A charge you don't recognize is easiest to
fight when you find it early. If an unauthorized withdrawal shows up on your
statement, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says you should

[tell your bank within 60 days](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-get-my-money-back-after-i-discover-an-unauthorized-transaction-or-money-missing-from-my-bank-account-en-1017/). If you wait longer, you could end up
paying for charges that happen after that.
You catch mistakes, the bank's and your own. A double charge, a refund that
never came, a fee you didn't expect, or a $54 purchase you wrote down as $45.
You stop trusting the wrong number. The balance your banking app shows may not
include everything that's on its way out. The federal agency that oversees
national banks [points out](https://www.helpwithmybank.gov/help-topics/bank-accounts/nsf-fees-overdraft-protection/nsf-fees/nsf-deposit-pending.html) that many transactions are processed
overnight, so they may not show up in your available balance yet. Checks that
haven't been cashed and payments still pending are already spent, as far as
you're concerned. If you spend against a number that doesn't know about them,
that's how overdraft fees happen.
And your budget is only as good as your record. Every total you look at later
depends on the transactions being right.
## How to do it
These steps follow the FDIC's Money Smart lesson,
[Balance your checkbook](https://www.fdic.gov/consumers/consumer/moneysmart/podcast/documents/mspn-2-3-checking-bal.pdf).
### 1. Get the statement
You need the ending balance and the list of everything on the statement. Most
banks show both online, and many let you download the list as a file.
### 2. Check off what matches
Go down the statement and find each item in your own record. Mark it in both
places. A pen works, and so does a column in a spreadsheet.
### 3. Look at what doesn't match
Whatever is left falls into two piles.
The first pile is things on the statement but not in your record. These might
be fees, interest, an automatic payment you forgot, or a charge you don't
recognize. Add the real ones to your record, and look into any you don't
recognize.
The second pile is things in your record but not on the statement. Usually
these haven't reached the bank yet. Think of a check that hasn't been cashed, a
deposit you made after the statement closed, or a purchase that's still
pending.
### 4. Do the math
Start with the statement's ending balance. Subtract the withdrawals that are
still on their way out, and add the deposits that are still on their way in.
The answer should match the balance in your own record.

**Diagram: In this example, the bank says $1,200, but a $250 check hasn’t been cashed and a $100 deposit hasn’t arrived. Allow for both, and $1,050 is what your record should say.** An example in four bars on one scale. The statement’s ending balance is $1,200. Take away $250 that’s still on its way out, which brings it to $950. Add $100 that’s still on its way in. That leaves $1,050, which should match the balance in your own record. Written out: $1,200 − $250 + $100 = $1,050.
### 5. If it doesn't match, look at the difference
How big the gap is gives you a clue:
- If it matches one transaction exactly, that one is missing from one side.
- If it's twice one transaction, that one was probably entered backward, as
money in instead of money out.
- If it divides evenly by 9, two digits were probably swapped. A $54 purchase
written as $45 leaves a gap of $9, and $820 written as $280 leaves $540.
Accountants look for this [when they reconcile](https://www.accountingtools.com/articles/transposition-error).

**Diagram: When two digits trade places, the gap always divides evenly by 9.** Two examples of swapped digits. First, the bank says $54 and you wrote $45: the 5 and the 4 traded places, and the gap is $9, which is 9 times 1. Second, the bank says $820 and you wrote $280: the 8 and the 2 traded places, the 0 stayed put, and the gap is $540, which is 9 times 60.
### 6. Do it every month
The best time is right after your statement comes, while you still remember
the month. Once it's a habit, it takes about ten minutes.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
### Bring in the statement
Download the statement period from your bank as a CSV file, then open
[**Import CSV**](https://smpl.money/docs/importing-a-statement/). Rows that look like something
you've already entered get flagged as possible duplicates. Each one is shown
side by side with the entry it looks like, so bringing in purchases you already
typed won't count them twice. Check the rows on
[**Staged**](https://smpl.money/docs/staged-transactions/), then press **Commit selected**.

![Staged transactions, the review queue: four rows that don't count yet, each with a date, payee, account, category, a Ready status and an amount, including a $19.99 refund from Streamly and a $23.50 transit pass on the travel card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/staged-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Open the register
On [**Accounts**](https://smpl.money/docs/accounts/#check-a-balance-against-your-statement), open
the account and press **Show register**. It lists every deposit and withdrawal
in date order, with the balance before and after each one. It's your own record,
laid out the same way as the bank's.

![The accounts page: a search box and sort controls, then accounts grouped by type. Under Checking, a euro account at €1,621.10 and Everyday Checking at $7,663.45. Under Savings, Savings at $20,200.00. Under Credit card, a card named Travel Card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/accounts-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Compare the closing balance
Find the last row on or before the statement's closing date. The balance after
that row should match the statement's ending balance, once you've allowed for
anything still on its way.
### Find where it went wrong
If they don't match, read down the register until its running balance stops
matching the bank's. That's the row to fix. The size of the gap tells you what
to look for, just like in step 5.
### Fix it and keep the history
On the same page, find that transaction in the list and press its pencil
button to correct it.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
Simple Balance records a fix as a change on top of the original instead of
erasing it. The history of the mistake stays, and
[**Activity**](https://smpl.money/docs/activity-history/) lists the change.
![The activity history, newest first: staged rows created and budget plans created, each with the date and time it happened.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/activity-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
> **What Simple Balance can't see.** Simple Balance doesn't pull anything from your bank today, so it only knows
> what you've brought in or typed. It doesn't know about holds, pending charges,
> or what your bank calls your available balance. And money you date in the
> future doesn't count toward any balance until that date comes.
## Sources

- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [How do I get my money back after I discover an unauthorized transaction or money missing from my bank account?](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-get-my-money-back-after-i-discover-an-unauthorized-transaction-or-money-missing-from-my-bank-account-en-1017/). Reviewed August 28, 2026.

- Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, HelpWithMyBank.gov. [Can the bank charge an overdraft fee while there is a deposit pending?](https://www.helpwithmybank.gov/help-topics/bank-accounts/nsf-fees-overdraft-protection/nsf-fees/nsf-deposit-pending.html).
- Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. [Money Smart podcast: Balance your checkbook](https://www.fdic.gov/consumers/consumer/moneysmart/podcast/documents/mspn-2-3-checking-bal.pdf).
- Steven Bragg, AccountingTools. [Transposition error definition](https://www.accountingtools.com/articles/transposition-error). February 13, 2026.

articles.title: How to budget with a credit card
articles.description: A card purchase is spending the day you make it, though the money leaves later. How to budget so the bill is never a surprise, and why to pay it in full.
steps: Add the card as an account
Record the payment as a transfer
lines: # How to budget with a credit card
> A card purchase is spending the day you make it, though the money leaves later. How to budget so the bill is never a surprise, and why to pay it in full.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/budget-with-a-credit-card/. Updated 2026-10-25.
A credit card turns one purchase into two moments. You buy groceries on the
3rd, and the money leaves your checking account weeks later when you pay the
bill. To budget with a card, count the spending at the first moment, the day
you buy something.
## Why it matters
Card spending doesn't feel like spending. Nothing leaves your bank account at
the register, so it's easy to spend the same money twice in one month.
The bill shows up after the month is over. By the time you see the total, it's
too late to change how you spent that month.
Carrying a balance is expensive. In August 2026, card accounts that were
charged interest paid about 22% a year on average, according to the
[Federal Reserve](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/20261007/). A two-year personal loan averaged about 12%, and a
five-year new car loan about 7.5%. If you pay your full statement balance by
the due date, you usually
[pay no interest on purchases at all](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/).

**Diagram: A card balance costs much more than other common loans. Pay the full statement balance by the due date and you usually pay no interest on purchases.** Average yearly interest rates in August 2026, from the Federal Reserve, as bars. Card accounts that were charged interest: about 22%. A two-year personal loan: about 12%. A five-year new car loan: about 7.5%. Below a dashed line, set apart because it isn’t an average: a card paid in full by the due date usually charges no interest on purchases.
It's also easy to count the same groceries twice. If you count the purchase
and then the card payment as spending, every total you look at is too high.
## Three numbers on your bill
Card statements show three numbers that sound alike:
- **Statement balance**: what you owed on the day the statement closed.
- **Current balance**: what you owe today, including anything you've bought
since the statement closed.
- **Minimum payment**: the least you can pay without a late fee. If you only
pay this, you'll be charged interest on the rest.
Paying the **statement balance** in full by the due date keeps your grace
period. That's the time between the end of the billing cycle and the due date,
when many cards charge no interest on purchases. Card companies
[don't have to offer one](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/credit-cards/answers/key-terms/), though, and it usually doesn't cover cash
advances. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says cash advances
[start charging interest right away](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/). Check your card's terms to be
sure.

**Diagram: The groceries count as spending on the 3rd. Paying the bill weeks later is a transfer from checking, so it doesn’t count again.** A timeline, top to bottom. On the 3rd, you buy $80 of groceries on the card, and it counts as grocery spending that day. At the end of the billing cycle, the statement closes. In this example the groceries are the only thing on the card, so the statement balance is $80. Then the grace period runs until the due date, and many cards charge no interest on purchases during it. On the due date, you pay the $80 from checking. That’s a transfer between your own accounts, not spending.
## How to do it
### 1. Count a purchase when you make it
Groceries bought on the card are grocery spending, on the day you buy them.
That's when you made the choice to spend.
### 2. Keep the cash for it
When you spend $80 on the card, $80 of your checking balance now belongs to
the card company. Think of it as gone, even though it hasn't left yet. If your
budget says you have grocery money left, that money has to really be there
when the bill comes.
### 3. Don't count the payment as spending
Paying the card from checking just moves money between your own accounts. The
spending already happened when you used the card. If you count the payment
too, you've counted it twice.
### 4. Pay the statement balance in full
If your card lets you, set up an automatic payment for the full statement
balance, not the minimum.
### 5. If you already carry a balance
First, stop adding to it. Use a debit card for new spending for a while. Then
budget a set payment above the minimum each month, and keep an eye on the
balance as it goes down. Watching it shrink makes it easier to keep going.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
### Add the card as an account
On [**Accounts**](https://smpl.money/docs/accounts/#credit-cards-and-loans), press **New account**
and choose **Credit card**. Type what you owe as a plain number, and leave
**Starting balance type** on **Amount owed**. The account starts below zero,
because that's money you owe, not money you have.

![The accounts page: a search box and sort controls, then accounts grouped by type. Under Checking, a euro account at €1,621.10 and Everyday Checking at $7,663.45. Under Savings, Savings at $20,200.00. Under Credit card, a card named Travel Card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/accounts-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Record purchases on the card
Each purchase is a **Withdrawal** from the card account, with a category. It
counts as spending in that category on the day you made it.
### Record the payment as a transfer
Paying the card from checking is a **Transfer** from checking to the card. A
transfer has no category and never shows up as spending, so nothing gets counted
twice. If you pay on the same day each month, save it on
[**Recurring**](https://smpl.money/docs/recurring-transactions/), and it'll be ready for you when
it's due. In the transaction list, a transfer shows both accounts and no
category, like the $600 one here.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Make interest easy to see
If your card charges interest or a fee, record it as a withdrawal from the
card with its own category, like Interest and fees. It's real spending.
Seeing it on its own line each month is a good reason to pay in full.
### How budgets count the card
In a budget that carries over, card spending empties the envelope the day you
swipe, even though no cash has moved yet. **Left to assign** counts what you
owe on the card, too. That keeps your budget from thinking you have more to
spend than you do.
On [**Budgets**](https://smpl.money/docs/budgets/), a budget carries over when you check **Carry
what is left over into the next month**.

![The budgets screen: a form for setting one, with fields for the category, the amount and how it's decided, the currency, a start date and an optional end date, an optional savings goal and which budget gets funded first, and a checkbox for carrying what's left into next month. Below it, the list of standing budgets begins with $200 a month for dining out.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/budgets-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Why two reports disagree
[**Reports**](https://smpl.money/docs/reports/) has both an **Income and expenses** report and a
**Cash flow** report, and with a card they won't match. A purchase counts as an
expense the day you swipe, but the cash leaves when you pay the bill. Both are
right. They just answer different questions.
### Find your statement balance
Open the card account and press **Show register**. The balance on the
statement's closing date should match what your statement says.
## Sources
- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. [Consumer Credit, G.19](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/20261007/). Release of October 7, 2026, with rates for August 2026.

- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [What is a grace period for a credit card?](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/). Reviewed September 23, 2024.
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. [Key terms](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/credit-cards/answers/key-terms/), from its credit card answers.

articles.title: How to find and keep track of your subscriptions
articles.description: Go through a year of bank and card statements and list every charge that repeats. Then decide on each one, and keep the list from growing back.
