lines: # How to find and keep track of your subscriptions
> Go through a year of bank and card statements and list every charge that repeats. Then decide on each one, and keep the list from growing back.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/find-your-subscriptions/. Updated 2026-10-25.
Subscriptions are easy to start and easy to forget. Each one is small, most
renew on their own, and a free trial turns into a charge on a date nobody wrote
down. To find them, go through a year of bank and card statements and list every
charge that repeats. That takes about an hour. Keeping the list short takes a
habit.
## Why it matters
People tend to guess low. In a [2022 survey by C+R Research](https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/), people's
first guess at what they spent on subscriptions each month averaged $86. When
they went through them one kind at a time, the average came to $219. That's
[$133 more](https://www.cnbc.com/2022/09/06/consumers-underestimate-monthly-subscription-costs-by-at-least-100.html) than they first thought. Both numbers came from what people
remembered, not from their statements, so the only way to know your real
number is to look.

**Diagram: On average, people first guessed they spent $86 a month on subscriptions. When they went through them one kind at a time, the average came to $219.** Two bars on the same scale, from a 2022 survey by C+R Research of what people spend on subscriptions each month, on average. The first bar is the average first guess: $86. The second bar is the average they came to when they went through them one kind at a time: $219. The first $86 of the second bar lines up with the guess, and the rest of it, $133, is marked as the part they missed.
They add up over a year. A $15 subscription you don't use costs $180 a year.
Three of those could pay for a weekend away.
Prices can creep up. A subscription can renew at a higher price than the one
you signed up for, with an email about it that you may never have opened.
Yearly renewals are the easiest to miss. A charge that comes once a year won't
show up in a month or two of statements, and when it does come, it's all at
once.
## How to do it
### 1. Pull a year of statements
Two or three months will show the monthly charges. A full year shows the
yearly ones too. Include every checking account and every card, plus any
online payment account you use.

**Diagram: A few months of statements will catch every monthly charge. Only a full year catches the one that comes once a year.** A year laid out as twelve months, January to December. A monthly charge shows up in every month. A yearly charge shows up once, in May. The last 3 months, October to December, are shaded: they hold three of the monthly charges and none of the yearly one. A bracket under all twelve months marks a full year, which holds both.
### 2. Look for repeats
Look for the same name or the same amount coming up month after month. Watch
for words like subscription, membership, renewal and premium. Also look for
app store charges, which can bundle many subscriptions under one name. Your
phone's app store account lists the subscriptions it bills you for.
### 3. Make a list
For each subscription, write down what it is, how much it costs, how often you
pay, when it renews, and which card it's on.
### 4. Decide on each one
Keep it, switch to a cheaper plan, or cancel it. If you haven't used it in a
month and wouldn't miss it, that's your answer. Cancel through the company's
own website or app, and save the confirmation.
### 5. Keep the list from growing back
Before you start a free trial, write down the date it turns into a charge and
set a reminder for a few days before. The Federal Trade Commission's advice on
[free trials and auto-renewals](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/getting-and-out-free-trials-auto-renewals-and-negative-option-subscriptions) is blunt: if you don't cancel on time,
you'll probably be charged. It also suggests watching your card statements
after you cancel, in case the charges keep coming. Then look over your list
every few months.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
Simple Balance isn't a subscription tracker that finds them for you, and it
can't cancel anything.
What it does give you is one place to see every payment, and a way to keep the
subscriptions you keep in plain view.
### Start with your payees
[**Payees**](https://smpl.money/docs/categories-and-payees/#payees) lists everyone you've paid,
with how many transactions each one has. Open one to see every payment you've
made to them. That's often how a monthly charge you forgot about turns up.

![The payees page: a search box and sort controls above a list of the people and businesses you've paid or been paid by, each with how many transactions it has, such as Greenline Market with 15.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/payees-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Search for the rest
On [**Transactions**](https://smpl.money/docs/transactions/#find-a-transaction), you can search by
payee, description or notes, and sort by any column. Sorting by amount puts
charges of the same size next to each other. That's a quick way to spot one that
repeats under slightly different names.

![A list of transactions, newest first, each with who it was with, which account it was in, its category and its amount, all in dollars. Most are spending on groceries, a lunch, cinema tickets and a transit pass. One is a $750 freelance payment coming in, and one is $600 moved from checking to savings, which shows both accounts and no category.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/transactions-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Put them in one category
Make a category called Subscriptions. On **Transactions**, check the rows that
belong in it and change their category all at once. The **Categories** report
under [**Reports**](https://smpl.money/docs/reports/) then shows what they cost together.

![The categories page: a form for a new category with its name, what it applies to and its group, a panel for making groups with no groups yet, and the list of categories below, each with its type, how many transactions use it and a group picker, starting with Dining out, Freelance and Groceries.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/categories-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Track the ones you keep
For each subscription you keep, open the menu on one of its transactions and
choose **Save as recurring transaction**. Your
[**Recurring**](https://smpl.money/docs/recurring-transactions/) page becomes your subscription
list. Each one adds a row to [**Staged**](https://smpl.money/docs/staged-transactions/) when it's
due, for you to check and approve, and it can send you an email when it does.

![The recurring page before anything is set up: a New recurring transaction button, and a note that each due date puts a row on Staged transactions for you to check.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/recurrences-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Get a reminder before a trial ends
A [**template**](https://smpl.money/docs/templates/#email-reminders) can send you an email
reminder on a single date. Make one for the trial, set the reminder for a few
days before the first charge, and you'll hear about it while you can still
cancel.
## Sources
- C+R Research. [Subscription service statistics and costs](https://www.crresearch.com/blog/subscription-service-statistics-and-costs/). Survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers, April and May 2022.

- Sarah Agostino, CNBC. [Most consumers underestimate monthly subscription costs by at least $100, study says](https://www.cnbc.com/2022/09/06/consumers-underestimate-monthly-subscription-costs-by-at-least-100.html). September 6, 2022.

- Federal Trade Commission. [Getting in and out of free trials, auto-renewals, and negative option subscriptions](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/getting-and-out-free-trials-auto-renewals-and-negative-option-subscriptions). September 2024.

lines: # What is net worth, and how do you calculate it?
> Net worth is what you own minus what you owe. How to add yours up, what to leave out, why it can start below zero, and why the trend matters most.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/net-worth/. Updated 2026-10-25.
Your net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. It's a single
number, and it answers a question a budget can't: over months and years, are
you getting ahead?
## What it is
**Net worth = what you own − what you owe.**
That's how [FINRA](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investing-basics/financial-foundations), the group that oversees brokerage firms in the U.S.,
explains it too: add up what you own, then subtract what you owe.
What you own includes cash, checking and savings, retirement and investment
accounts, and things you could sell, like a home or a car. What you owe
includes credit card balances, student loans, a car loan, a mortgage, medical
bills, and anything else you're paying off.
Say you have $8,000 in checking and savings and a car worth $6,000. You owe
$2,000 on a credit card and $15,000 in student loans. You own $14,000 and owe
$17,000, so your net worth is **−$3,000**.

**Diagram: Net worth is the gap between the two bars. In the article’s example, what you owe is bigger, so it comes out below zero.** Two bars on the same scale. What you own: $8,000 in checking and savings and a car worth $6,000, $14,000 in all. What you owe: $2,000 on a credit card and $15,000 in student loans, $17,000 in all. The second bar is $3,000 longer, so net worth is minus $3,000.
Don't panic if yours comes out below zero. Early on, a student loan can be
bigger than everything you own. What matters is which way the number moves.
## Why it matters
Net worth shows progress that a budget can't. A budget tells you about this
month. Net worth tells you whether the months are adding up to something.

**Diagram: An example: still below zero after six months, but higher every month. The direction is the part to watch.** An example line chart of net worth over six months, from January to June: minus $3,000, minus $2,600, minus $2,100, minus $1,900, minus $1,300 and minus $800. Every point is below the zero line, and every month is higher than the one before.
It counts paying off debt. Paying $500 off a loan doesn't feel like saving, but
your net worth goes up by the same $500 as if you'd put it in the bank.
It also catches slow leaks. Spending a little more than you earn each month
won't jump out of any one month's budget, but it shows up as a net worth that
slowly drops.
Your own trend tells you more than any comparison. Measuring your number
against a friend's, or a headline's, doesn't tell you much. Measuring it
against your own number from six months ago does.
> **About those average net worth numbers.** The Federal Reserve's [2025 Survey of Consumer Finances](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20261009a.htm), released
> in October 2026, put the median family's net worth at $215,900 and the mean at
> $1.24 million, both in 2025 dollars. The median is the family right in the
> middle. The mean gets pulled up by a small number of very wealthy families, so
> the median gives a better picture of a typical household. When you see a
> headline about net worth, check which one it's using. Both numbers are per
> family, not per person, and the [full report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf) breaks them down by
> age.
## How to do it
### 1. List what you own
Use today's balance for every account. For a retirement or investment account,
use what it's worth today. For a home or a car, use what it would really sell
for, not what you paid. If you're not sure, leave something like a car out. A
number that's a little low is more useful than one that makes you feel good.
Don't count everyday things like furniture or clothes. You can't easily turn
them back into money.
### 2. List what you owe
Use the full amount of every debt, not the monthly payment. That means the
whole credit card balance and the whole loan.
### 3. Subtract
Take what you own minus what you owe. Write the answer down with the date.
### 4. Do it again the same way
Once a month or once every three months is plenty. Use the same rules each
time, like whether the car counts, so the change from one date to the next
means something.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
Simple Balance works as a net worth tracker. Once every account is in it, one
report adds them all up for you.
### Add every account
On [**Accounts**](https://smpl.money/docs/accounts/), press **New account** for each account you
have, including the ones that hold debt. For a debt, choose **Credit card** or
**Loan**. Type what you owe as a plain number and leave **Starting balance
type** on **Amount owed**. The account starts below zero, which is exactly how
it counts toward your net worth.

![The accounts page: a search box and sort controls, then accounts grouped by type. Under Checking, a euro account at €1,621.10 and Everyday Checking at $7,663.45. Under Savings, Savings at $20,200.00. Under Credit card, a card named Travel Card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/accounts-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Read the report
[**Reports**](https://smpl.money/docs/reports/#net-worth) has a **Net worth** report that adds up
what your accounts hold and what they owe. Group it by month or by quarter to
see the trend, not just one number.

![A net worth report with a separate table for each currency: checking, savings and a credit card totaled in dollars, and below it a euro account totaled in euros. No combined number appears anywhere.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/reports-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### More than one currency
If you have money in more than one currency, Simple Balance totals each one
separately and never converts between them. Any exchange rate it picked would
be out of date by tomorrow.
### Things it can't put a price on
Simple Balance doesn't look up what investments, a home or a car are worth.
You can keep them as accounts of type **Investment** or **Other asset**, but
their balances are only as up to date as the last value you entered. You can
also track just your cash and debts here and leave the rest out. That's a fine
net worth to watch, as long as you count it the same way every time.
### Accounts you've closed
You can archive an account you've closed from its row menu. Its history stays
there for you to read, and its balance stops counting toward your totals.
## Sources
- FINRA. [Financial Foundations](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investing-basics/financial-foundations).

- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. [Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20261009a.htm). Press release, October 9, 2026.
- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. [Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf). October 2026.

articles.title: How much should you have in an emergency fund?
articles.description: Three to six months of expenses is the usual answer. What counts as an emergency, how to work out your own number, and how to build the fund a step at a time.

lines: # How much should you have in an emergency fund?
> Three to six months of expenses is the usual answer. What counts as an emergency, how to work out your own number, and how to build the fund a step at a time.
From Simple Balance: https://smpl.money/learn/emergency-fund/. Updated 2026-10-25.
An emergency fund is money you set aside for things you can't plan for, like
losing a job, a medical bill, or a car repair you need to get to work. The
Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis and FINRA both suggest saving three to six
months of essential expenses. With an emergency fund, a bad month stays a bad
month. Without one, it can turn into a debt you're still paying off a year
later.
## Why it matters
Without savings, emergencies go on credit cards. A $1,200 car repair becomes a
card balance, and the interest makes that repair cost more every month it
isn't paid off.
Lots of people don't have that cushion. In the Federal Reserve's
[survey of household finances for 2025](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm), 63% of adults said they'd
cover a surprise $400 expense with cash or its equivalent. That includes
paying with a credit card and paying it off in full. So more than a third would
have to borrow, sell something, or couldn't cover it at all.

**Diagram: Each dot stands for one adult out of 100. More than a third would have to borrow, sell something, or couldn’t cover a surprise $400 expense at all.** A grid of 100 dots, one for each of 100 adults, from the Federal Reserve’s survey for 2025. The first 63 dots are solid green: 63% would cover a surprise $400 expense with cash or its equivalent. The rest are amber rings: more than a third would have to borrow, sell something, or couldn’t cover it at all.
An emergency fund protects everything else, too. One bad week can wipe out a
budget, a plan to pay off debt, or a savings goal. The fund keeps those plans
on track.
It also buys you time. If you lose your job with three months of expenses in
the bank, you can look for the right next job instead of grabbing the first
one.
## How much
The usual rule of thumb is **three to six months of essential expenses**. The

[Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis](https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/page-one-economics/2025/sep/when-unexpected-happens-be-ready-with-emergency-fund) and [FINRA](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/how-avoid-bad-financial-luck-friday-13th) both give that
range. That's expenses, not income: what it costs to keep a roof over your
head, the lights on, food on the table, and the minimum payments made.
Where you land in that range depends on how long it would take to replace your
income. The St. Louis Fed describes the fund as what pays your bills "while
you're searching for the next job." If your work is irregular, or yours is the
only income in your home, finding new work could take longer. Aim closer to
six months.
**Start smaller.** Six months of expenses is a lot of money. Iowa's Department
of Insurance and Financial Services suggests [three steps](https://smarther.iowa.gov/emergency-savings-your-financial-safety-net/): save $500
first, then one month of expenses, then three months and beyond. The Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau's
[guide to building an emergency fund](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/start-small-save-up/start-saving/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/) makes the same point: even a
small amount helps.

**Diagram: Build it a step at a time: $500, then one month of expenses, then three. Three to six months is the usual goal.** Four steps rising from left to right, like stairs. Step one is $500, marked start here. Step two is one month of expenses. Step three is three months. Step four is six months. Steps three and four are marked as the usual goal: three to six months of essential expenses. The month steps are drawn to scale: three months is three times as tall as one, and six is twice as tall as three. $500 is drawn as the smallest step.
### What counts as an emergency
Losing income, medical and dental bills, urgent car or home repairs, and
emergency travel all count. The holidays, a vacation, and a yearly insurance
bill don't. You can see those coming, so they belong in
[sinking funds](https://smpl.money/learn/sinking-funds/) instead.
## How to do it
### 1. Work out your monthly essentials
Add up rent or mortgage, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation and
minimum debt payments for a recent month.
[Tracking your spending](https://smpl.money/learn/track-your-spending/) gives you a real number
instead of a guess.
### 2. Multiply
Three times that monthly number is your starting target. Six times is the
fuller goal.
### 3. Give it its own account
Keep the fund in a savings account, apart from the account you spend from. The
St. Louis Fed's advice is to keep it "available when you need it, but not too
easily available." It also notes that many people use a savings account at a
local bank or credit union.
### 4. Make it automatic
Set up a transfer on payday, even a small one. FINRA suggests starting with "a
regular, automatic contribution of an amount you can reliably afford," and
adding extra when you can. A tax refund or a bonus is a good time for that.
### 5. Refill it after you use it
Using it is what it's for. Afterward, go back to step 4 until it's full again.
## How to do it in Simple Balance
### Find your monthly essentials
[**Reports**](https://smpl.money/docs/reports/) has an **Income and expenses** report. Group it by
month and look at your expenses for the last three months. Or use
[**Overview**](https://smpl.money/docs/the-overview/) to see spending by category over the same
dates, and add up the essential ones.

![The Simple Balance overview for one month: a dollar total with balance, deposits, withdrawals and net cash flow across the top, then a checking account, a savings account and a credit card with their balances, beside spending by category as bars from rent down to subscriptions.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/dashboard-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Give the fund its own account
On [**Accounts**](https://smpl.money/docs/accounts/), add a **Savings** account for the fund. On
its form, turn off **The budget is about the money in this account**, so your
budget doesn't treat emergency money as money to spend. If you use left to
assign, moving money into the fund lowers it, and that's right: the money has a
job now.

![The accounts page: a search box and sort controls, then accounts grouped by type. Under Checking, a euro account at €1,621.10 and Everyday Checking at $7,663.45. Under Savings, Savings at $20,200.00. Under Credit card, a card named Travel Card.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/accounts-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Make the payday transfer repeat
On [**Recurring**](https://smpl.money/docs/recurring-transactions/), press **New recurring
transaction** and set up a **Transfer** from checking to the fund on your
payday. Each time it's due, a row shows up in
[**Staged**](https://smpl.money/docs/staged-transactions/) for you to approve once the money has
really moved. It never posts on its own.

![The recurring page before anything is set up: a New recurring transaction button, and a note that each due date puts a row on Staged transactions for you to check.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/recurrences-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._
### Watch it grow
You'll see the fund's balance on **Accounts**, and it counts toward your **Net
worth** report like any other account. When you use it, record a transfer
back to checking. Then record what you spent it on in its own category, so
your reports show what the emergency really was.

![A net worth report with a separate table for each currency: checking, savings and a credit card totaled in dollars, and below it a euro account totaled in euros. No combined number appears anywhere.](https://smpl.money/screenshots/reports-light.webp)
_The money in this picture is made up. It's the real product, filled with
example spending._

- Scott A. Wolla, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. [When the Unexpected Happens, Be Ready with an Emergency Fund](https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/page-one-economics/2025/sep/when-unexpected-happens-be-ready-with-emergency-fund). _Page One Economics_, September 2, 2025.
